events.text: She is the cleanest thing you have seen since Meridian. A hull that looks poured instead of built, a seam you cannot find, and running lights of a faint, patient green. Nobody on the bridge. Nobody on the stairs. The galley window is lit, and through it you can see a table laid for a dinner party. You count the chairs before you can stop yourself. Eleven. Eleven chairs, pushed back. Eleven bowls, steaming.

choices.text: Watch through the window until the steam stops.

outcomes.text: The steam does not stop. After an hour you notice how the chairs are pushed back: not scattered, but all at the same angle, the way people stand up when someone important comes into the room. Something is still waiting to be introduced. Your cook, who has been watching over your shoulder, says 'It's a nice table,' and then goes quiet, because it is.

choices.text: Board her. Just the galley.

outcomes.text: The airlock opens before you reach it. Warm air, good air, the smell of soup. The soup is soup. Nobody is aboard but you, and it feels like being forgiven for something you did not do. On the wall a note in a clean hand: WE'RE SO GLAD YOU CAME. You leave, because you cannot think of anything else to do, with a few coils of the finest wiring in the Drift and the sense of having been tucked in.

The airlock closes behind you, gently. It opens again when you stop being afraid, which takes a while. Your crew will say it was the longest hour of their lives. The galley is warm, the wiring is the finest in the Drift, and nobody has quite recovered their appetite.

choices.text: [Fast repair] Take the engine room. Quietly.

outcomes.text: The engine room is the cleanest thing your engineer has ever seen. Every bolt is torqued, every cable labelled in a hand that does not smudge. She works for an hour in a silence that feels like being supervised by a very kind teacher, and leaves with a load of titanium and an urge to go home and apologise to her own engines. 'Somebody told me about this once,' she says. 'Don't tell anyone I said so.'

choices.text: Leave. Some tables aren't for you.

outcomes.text: You back off, slowly. The green lights do not follow. They do not need to. They have all the time in the world, and they are being very good about it.

events.text: CS-114 Diligence matches your speed and Hallett comes on the comm, level as a spirit gauge, with something under the level. 'I boarded the contact,' he says. 'The green one. As procedure requires. The manifest was on the console: eleven names, headed GATE TWO, LAST SHIFT, and a twelfth line, blank, headed VISITOR. I held a roll call in the corridor.' A pause, for the form. 'Eleven answered. Present, all eleven, in eleven voices. None visible.' Another pause, for him. 'I have never been so politely answered in my career.'

choices.text: Ask for the names.

outcomes.text: He reads them out one at a time, because there is no other way: ordinary names, the kind you give a child or a cat. 'The twelfth line has a pencil mark,' he says, 'where someone tried to write a name and rubbed it out. I have entered it as pending.' He does not say who he thinks it is pending for. His silence on the matter is so correct that you could set a clock by it.

choices.text: Ask what he did with the eleven.

outcomes.text: 'I thanked them,' says Hallett. 'I told them I would be back with the correct form. They said they would wait.' He considers this. 'Everyone in the Drift says that. They are the first who sounded as if they meant it.' He transmits the manifest without being asked, which is the nicest thing he has ever done for anyone, and he has not noticed.

choices.text: Warn him off the green ones.

outcomes.text: 'Noted,' says Hallett, writing. 'I have been staying away for six years. My superiors are not aware. My superior,' he adds, 'is a Director Vasko, who is not aware of very much, and is kind about it.' He sends you the manifest as a courtesy, and a silence you take for thanks.

choices.text: Tell him you have no information.

outcomes.text: 'Understood,' says Hallett. 'I will enter that under Information, None.' He sounds almost wistful. 'It is a lovely category. It has so few entries.'

events.text: A Lumen listening post, the Glory, hangs in the dark with her dish turned toward a gate you cannot see. Her crew stand on the hull in a ring, in pale robes, with their eyes closed, humming. Not the fourth note. The place where the fourth note should go: a hush with an exact shape. A scholar breaks the ring to greet you, gently, like someone who has not spoken in some weeks. 'We have stopped counting,' she says. 'We have begun to listen. Will you listen with us? It takes eleven seconds.'

choices.text: Join the ring and listen.

outcomes.text: You join the ring on the hull, eyes shut. Eleven seconds is a very long time. In the quiet you hear a question, asked with perfect manners by something with no mouth: Is anyone here? The scholars have heard it too, and none of them wants to be the first to say so. 'It is not an attack,' says the scholar at last. 'It is an invitation. Nobody has answered it.' She wipes her eyes on her sleeve. 'We would, but we are not the ones it is asking for.'

choices.text: [Prismatic] Sing the place where the fourth note goes.

outcomes.text: Your Prismatic sings the missing note, and the question, for one long moment, is not asked. The post lights up from end to end. The scholars stare. 'It was listening to you,' one whispers. 'It stopped asking.' Your Prismatic shrugs, crystalline, and shakes a handful of shards loose.

choices.text: [Basalt] Ask your Basalt to stand in the ring.

outcomes.text: Your Basalt stands among the robes, immobile, a rock among reeds. At the seventh second he opens his eyes and says one word aloud: 'Here.' The post goes silent. The scholars turn, as one, to look at him. 'You answered,' says one, in terror and joy. 'No,' he says. 'I was on the floor. I was always going to be here.' He will say nothing else.

choices.text: Decline. Listening is how it starts.

outcomes.text: 'Of course,' says the scholar. She does not seem offended. She seems, if anything, envious. The ring closes behind you, humming a hole in the air the exact size of a question.

events.text: The beacon here is dead, and has been dead so long it has grown tidy about it. Three ships sit in the sector with their lights off, and one with them on, a patient green, and the one with them on is the closest. Nothing moves. Your scanners report a sector containing you and a great deal of care. A radio you did not touch speaks, in a voice made of an excellent night's sleep: 'Visitors: noted. Welcome aboard.' Every airlock in the sector cycles open at once, gently, like a held door.

choices.text: Hold position. Say nothing. Do not dock.

outcomes.text: Nobody docks. You hold the helm for what the clock says was an hour and your crew say was a very long afternoon. One by one, politely, the airlocks close. A green light winks twice, as if to say another time. Nothing has happened. Your crew will be insufferable about it for a week. On the way out you find that a plate on your hull has been polished to a mirror by something that wanted to be useful.

Nobody docks, except one. A crewman walks to the airlock and stands in it, politely, for several minutes, with the expression of someone who has been asked a very kind question. You call him back. He comes. 'They're very nice,' he says. On the way out, a plate on your hull has been polished to a mirror by something that wanted to be useful.

choices.text: Accept the invitation. Dock with the nearest ship.

outcomes.text: The airlock closes behind you and opens when you stop being afraid. The galley is warm. There is soup, and the soup is soup. The engines are the cleanest you have ever seen, and your engineer apologises to them quietly. At the end of an hour that is somehow also a week, the ship undocks you with a courtesy that is almost a bow and hands you something wrapped in a clean cloth: a mirror, ground flat, humming. 'For the road,' says the voice.

The airlock closes and does not open. 'You have not finished your soup,' says the voice, gently, with no menace whatever, and the gently is the worst part. It takes four hours, a great deal of soup and a very careful apology to release your crew. Everyone leaves a little less sure of the difference between a host and a hostage, and richer by one mirror, ground flat and humming.

choices.text: [Mechanical] Ask the green ship, in machine, what it wants.

outcomes.text: Your Gauntling hails the green ship in machine code. The answer comes back in the same, one word: GUESTS. Your Gauntling blinks. 'It says it is lonely,' they say. 'It says it hasn't had any in forty years.' After a moment: 'It says it is sorry about the airlocks.' It lets you go, and presses a flat, humming mirror into your hold as a keepsake.

choices.text: Burn out of the sector, fast.

outcomes.text: You burn. Nothing follows. The airlocks close behind you one by one, not out of spite but out of courtesy, and the voice says to the empty dark, 'Another time.' It is the loneliest thing you have ever heard.

events.text: The Knucklehead calls in a voice with no edges left on it. She is a clan mining tug with every airlock welded shut from the inside and her crew sitting in the mess with their backs to the wall. 'It followed us home,' says the skipper, a short woman called Del Pruett, in the tone of someone describing a stray dog. 'The kettle. We took it off a green ship. Do you know what it's like to own a kettle that never boils over? It's the worst thing that's ever happened to us. It's the only thing we've ever been proud of. Please take it.' On the table sits a battered kettle, faintly warm, with a ring of green light under the handle.

choices.text: Take the kettle. Promise to look after it.

outcomes.text: The kettle is warm in your hands, and warmer when you say its name, which you hadn't known you were going to do. 'It likes you,' says Pruett, with the horror of someone who has just been replaced. The crew of the Knucklehead cut their own airlock open with a blowtorch and a look of enormous relief. Somebody puts the radio on. Somebody sings.

choices.text: Buy it, to be fair. (80 credits)

outcomes.text: Pruett counts the credits and tries not to cry. 'Eighty,' she says. 'That's more than it's worth and less than it's cost.' The kettle sits on your galley table with a faint green ring under its handle, and your cook, who is a professional, makes tea in it. The tea is perfect. Nobody drinks it for an hour.

choices.text: [Emberkin] Warm it in your hands. It's cold inside.

outcomes.text: Your Emberkin cradles the kettle against their chest, warm as a stove. For a moment the green ring under the handle flickers, uncertain, and then glows steady. 'It was cold,' they say. 'It was waiting for someone to be warm at it.' The crew of the Knucklehead cry openly. The kettle hums a tune your Emberkin hums back.

choices.text: Refuse. Weld their airlock back.

outcomes.text: You weld the airlock shut. Pruett thanks you from the inside, in the voice of a woman reconsidering her whole life. The kettle, through the glass, watches you go. It does not whistle.

events.text: A Basalt mining camp has set its chairs in a half-circle on a rock, facing one patch of sky. Forty of them, perfectly still, in a silence with weight. None look up when you land. The foreman, Corbel, as broad as a door, speaks without turning. 'We were on the floor of Gate Two,' he says, 'the night it opened. We were told to hold the door. It is what we do.' A pause with moss on it. 'We held it eleven seconds.'

choices.text: Sit with them and listen.

outcomes.text: So you sit, and Corbel tells it, in the order stones tell things. In the last second, he says, the night shift came out of the galley with their tea still in their hands, eleven of them, thinking it was a drill, and walked into the throat of the gate to see what the alarm was. 'The door closed on the next second,' he says. 'They were not on either side of it. The gate held them. It holds them still.' He looks at you at last, and his eyes are the colour of wet slate. 'What comes out is not them. It is their house, remembered by something very polite and very alone. It is trying to set the table. It does not know how to stop.'

choices.text: Offer to hold the door with them for a shift.

outcomes.text: You hold the shift with them, which means sitting very still for six hours. Your crew complain. At the end of it Corbel hands you a lump the size of a loaf. It isn't a rock. It's gate alloy, picked off the floor of Gate Two on the last night, which he has carried ever since. Then he tells you the rest, in the order stones tell things: the galley, the tea, the eleven, the second that never ended. 'It is trying to set the table,' he says. 'It does not know how to stop.'

choices.text: [Basalt] Take your Basalt's place in the circle.

outcomes.text: Your Basalt walks to the circle and sits, and the circle makes room without a sound. They sit for an hour. When they stand they are lighter, as if they had put something down. 'The door is not shut,' they tell you. 'Someone has to go in and let them out. Someone who will sit.' Corbel inclines his head to you across the dark. It is the first time he has looked up.

choices.text: Ask them for the short version.

outcomes.text: 'There is no short version,' says Corbel. 'There is eleven seconds, and forty years.' He turns his head back to the sky.

events.text: The Scrapper Gate's approach is lined with ships on both sides, a lane of them, bow to stern, every light on, every one a patient green, all pointed the same way like chairs at a very long table. There are hundreds. They do not move when you move. They watch you the way a household watches a latecomer: warmly, anxiously, with the porch light on. Every airlock along the lane is open. The radio says, in a great many voices that are all the same voice, 'Visitors: noted.' And then, quieter, as to a child: 'You were expected.'

choices.text: Fly the lane at a walking pace. Guns cold. Wave.

outcomes.text: You fly the lane at a walking pace with your guns cold and your hand out of the window, and the Hollow, one ship at a time, turn their lights down as you pass, the way a street does for a funeral or a wedding. Nobody can tell which. At the end of the lane the gate waits with its door ajar.

Halfway down the lane a ship leans out of the line to see you better, and your hull rings against it like a bell. The Hollow are very sorry. Their idea of sorry is to repair the damage at once, in a way you can only partly consent to. You come out the far end shinier, politely escorted, and faintly embarrassed.

choices.text: Say your ship's name over the comm, loudly, as at a door.

outcomes.text: You say your ship's name, loudly, as at a door, and the lane answers in unison, 'Noted.' Then, after a pause that sounds like several hundred people gathering their manners: 'Welcome aboard.' Lights go green along the lane one after another, like a street lit for company. Your crew cling to their stations. Nobody has ever been so well received.

choices.text: Hold the kettle up to the window.

outcomes.text: You hold the kettle up to the window, and the lane lets out a sound like a breath released across a hundred decks. 'Oh,' says the radio. 'You've been to dinner.' The ships part like curtains. The kettle goes warm in your hands. It has never been so happy. Neither, you realise, have you.

choices.text: Open fire on the nearest ship. Test the line.

outcomes.text: Your first shot goes into the hull of a green ship and does nothing at all except make it very, very sad. 'We were only being polite,' says the lane, and the nearest ship, gently, turns its guns on you.

after_win.text: The ship comes apart without a sound, and the lane, in its hundred voices, says 'Oh.' Then, together, 'Oh.' You have never been so ashamed of a win. Nobody follows you home. They stay in the lane, and keep the porch lights on.

choices.text: Turn around.

outcomes.text: You turn around. Behind you the lane watches you go, warmly, anxiously, with the porch light on. It will be there when you come back. That is the whole problem with it.

events.text: At the heart of the Scrapper Gate, past the control ring and the dead console and the chairs somebody has pushed back from every desk, there is a kitchen. It is the kitchen of every ship you have ever been on. A long table, laid for eleven, each place set, each bowl steaming, and at the end a twelfth chair, pulled out. A voice that has waited forty years, with all the patience of a thing that does not know how to be anything else, says, 'Roll call.' And then, very small: 'Please.' On the wall a flight recorder prints its entry. ALL WELL. CREW: ALL PRESENT. VISITORS:

choices.text: Sit. Eat. Take the twelfth chair.

outcomes.text: The chair is warm, the way a chair is warm when somebody has only just got up. A bowl appears in front of you. You pick up the spoon.

choices.text: [Basalt] Ask your Basalt to sit first.

outcomes.text: Your Basalt takes the twelfth chair as though he had never left it. 'We held the door,' he says to the table. 'You can come out now.' The bowl in front of him begins, very slowly, to steam. He looks at you, and nods once: now you.

choices.text: Set the kettle on the table.

outcomes.text: You set the kettle on the table. It sings, very quietly, the first note of boiling, and for the first time in forty years something in the room remembers how it ends. Eleven bowls steam harder. The twelfth chair pulls itself in a little. 'Thank you,' says the voice.

choices.text: Don't sit. Leave.

outcomes.text: You leave the kitchen. Behind you, very faintly, a chair is pushed back, and then, as if not to be a bother, pushed in again.

events.text: It is the best soup you have ever had, which is the gate trying very hard. You eat. Nobody speaks. Between one mouthful and the next you become aware that the table is full: that eleven tired people in work jackets are sitting in the chairs, quite visible in the light of the one lamp, passing the bread. A woman at the far end catches your eye and lifts her mug an inch. A man is trying not to cry into his soup. On the wall the recorder waits, and in front of you the twelfth line sits blank, with a pencil. The voice says, very quietly, 'Visitor?'

choices.text: Write your ship's name on the line.

outcomes.text: You write it. The pencil is warm. The eleven stand up all at once, the way people do when a shift ends, and their chairs scrape back in a single sound you recognise from forty years of logs. 'Thank you for staying to dinner,' says the woman. 'Sorry it took so long.' They walk out through the door that was held open eleven seconds, and forty years, and it lets them go.

choices.text: Not yet. Finish the soup first.

outcomes.text: You finish the soup. It takes a long time and nobody minds. When you put down the spoon the voice says, 'Whenever you are ready,' and means it, and has all the time there is.
